canopy.name: Cardon
canopy.source: Pachycereus pringlei, Baja California and Sonora coast, giant columnar cactus 8-18 m — Flora of North America

traits.native_range: Pachycereus pringlei, Baja California and Sonora coast, giant columnar cactus 8-18 m — Flora of North America
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: massive grey-green column with several arms

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are pea-sized green globes with tiny spines, nearly always under a nurse shrub or tree. They elongate into a single thick, ribbed, grey-green column, much spinier than adults (old cardons can be almost spineless); after decades arms branch from low on the trunk and turn upward like a candelabra.
growth.source: Radiocarbon dating of cardon spines (Radiocarbon journal): growth 3-23 cm/yr, mean 9.8 cm/yr, faster in taller plants; Wikipedia (slow-growing, lifespan hundreds of years, tallest 19.2 m); El cardon gigante (Acta Universitaria 2017); age at first flowering estimated

fruiting.source: USA-NPN photo guide (milky-white flowers late spring; fruit turns reddish and splits to show red pulp; lesser long-nosed bats depend on its nectar); Nativas Landscape (flowers open late afternoon, die next day around noon); Acta Universitaria (flowering-fruiting Apr-Sep); fruit size, set and crop estimated

canopy.source: Aloidendron dichotomum, Namib and Namaqualand rocky slopes, forked succulent tree 3-9 m — SANBI PlantZAfrica

traits.native_range: Aloidendron dichotomum, Namib and Namaqualand rocky slopes, forked succulent tree 3-9 m — SANBI PlantZAfrica
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: forked golden trunk, rounded crown of rosettes

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a tiny fan of thick, triangular, blue-green leaves in two ranks, often pale-spotted and edged with small teeth, later twisting into a spiral rosette. For years it stays a squat rosette; then a single stout trunk lifts it and at 1-2 m the crown forks again and again into a rounded head of rosettes. Old bark peels in golden, sharp-edged plates.
growth.source: Wikipedia (slow growth, stems repeatedly fork in two) and SANBI PlantZAfrica as recalled (tree aloe to 7-9 m of Namibia and the Northern Cape; first flowers at about 20-30 yr; large trees thought well over a century old). Two-ranked spotted seedling leaves as in most aloes; rates estimated.

fruiting.source: German Wikipedia (Koecherbaum: 3-5-branched inflorescence to 30 cm with cylindrical racemes to 15 cm; bulbous flowers 33 mm long, bright canary-yellow; nectar favoured by sunbirds). Winter (Jun-Jul) flowering, bee visits, capsules with papery winged seeds, timings and crop estimated from SANBI as recalled and related tree aloes.

canopy.name: Umbrella thorn
canopy.origin: Africa (Sahel to South Africa) and Arabia

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval cotyledons, then tiny feathery bipinnate leaves on a thin stem with paired spines, some long, straight and white, others short and hooked. The taproot dives deep first. Browsed saplings become dense, low, cage-like spiny bushes for years; once a leader escapes browsers it gains about 1.5 m in two years and only later spreads the flat umbrella crown.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): up to 21 m, about 1.5 m in 2 years, a 6-7-year-old tree yields 5-6 kg of clean seed, 10-12 kg pods a year at 10 yr; Andersen & Krzywinski 2007 (BMC Ecology): radiocarbon ages of 200-650 yr for trees in Egypt's Eastern Desert, radial growth up to 2.4 mm a year. Germination and height curve estimated.

canopy.source: Sahel to South Africa savanna; the flat-top. Kew POWO (African acacias are now Vachellia/Senegalia; Acacia is the Australian wattles). Thorny (African), flat crowns, insect-pollinated, pods eaten by browsers which spread the seed; giraffe and goat browse; fire-adapted.

traits.leaf_shape: compound or lobed leaves in a flat spreading crown
traits.trunk: single trunk, flat-topped crown or, for herbs, a huge single leaf on a stalk
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: grey to black-brown, rough and fissured; young twigs reddish; paired thorns: long straight white ones and short hooked ones

leaf.notes: tiny feathery bipinnate leaves, minute leaflets; foliage fine grey-green haze

flower.form: small creamy-white fluffy balls in clusters

fruit.form: pale yellow-brown pods twisted into tight spirals and coils, 8-12 cm; fall for browsers

appearance.seasonal: drops leaves in the long dry season; flushes with rains
appearance.silhouette: the flat-top: a wide, perfectly flat or slightly domed umbrella crown on a short trunk or several leaning stems; the savanna signature
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Vachellia tortilis; Kew POWO; PlantZAfrica

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): white or pale yellowish-white heads 0.5-1.1 cm, pods 7-10 cm by 6-10 mm, spirally twisted, 10-12 kg pods per 10-yr tree; the Turkana make porridge from the pods, the Maasai eat immature seeds; Wikipedia: aromatic flowers, springlike coiled pods. Flowering at the onset of the rains, ripening, pod fall and rot times estimated.

shrub.name: Whitethorn acacia
shrub.source: Vachellia constricta, Sonoran/Chihuahuan deserts, thorny shrub 1-4 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.native_range: Vachellia constricta, Sonoran/Chihuahuan deserts, thorny shrub 1-4 m — USDA PLANTS
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Hard-coated seeds germinate after summer rains once the coat is cracked: two thick oval cotyledons, a first once-pinnate leaf, then tiny bipinnate leaves on a slender reddish stem with a pair of straight white spines at each node. A deep taproot grows first; the plant soon branches from the base into a low, open, spiny shrublet with zigzag red-brown twigs.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Vachellia constricta): usually 2 m, occasionally 6 m, flowers Apr-May with a second bloom Jul-Oct. Germination, growth, first flowering and lifespan estimated from related Sonoran and Chihuahuan desert acacias.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (Vachellia constricta): blooms Apr-May and again Jul-Oct, small yellow balls about 1 cm offering no nectar and little pollen; pods long and thin, up to 12 cm by 3-6 mm. Red-brown colour, constriction between seeds and splitting per the species' usual description; fruit set, timings and crop estimated.

shrub.name: Barrel cactus
shrub.source: Ferocactus wislizeni, Sonoran/Chihuahuan deserts, barrel 0.5-1.5 m, hooked red spines — Flora of North America

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: a tiny green knob with two fleshy cotyledons, soon covered in fine white spines; stays a small spiny globe for years (often in the shade of a nurse shrub), growing a few cm a year and gaining its hooked reddish central spines. At 20-30 cm across it starts to flower; it lengthens into a ribbed barrel and, when tall, leans toward the south-southwest.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Ferocactus wislizeni: germination best at 20-30 C with >=8 h light; lifespan 50-130 yr); Wikipedia (0.9-1.8 m, rarely 3 m; 50-100 yr). Growth rate and first flowering estimated from barrel-cactus growth.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (flowers sporadically in late spring, profusely Jul-Sep; fruit yellow, barrel-shaped, fleshy); Wikipedia (yellow to red-orange flowers visited by cactus bees Lithurgus; fruits persist atop the plant, sometimes >1 yr; eaten by deer, javelina, ground squirrels; sour but edible). Flower size, counts, ripening estimated.

ground.name: Lechuguilla
ground.source: Agave lechuguilla, indicator of the Chihuahuan Desert, spiky rosettes 30-60 cm — USDA PLANTS

traits.native_range: Agave lechuguilla, indicator of the Chihuahuan Desert, spiky rosettes 30-60 cm — USDA PLANTS
traits.leaf_shape: stiff spined sword leaves in a rosette
traits.trunk: none or a short woody stem; tall flower spike
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are rarely seen; nearly all young rosettes are pups rising from rhizomes about 10 cm down, spreading 2-3 times the parent's width, so plants form dense colonies. A young rosette is a tight upright cup of a few stiff, thick, yellow-green, slightly incurved leaves with small down-hooked edge teeth and a sharp tip spine; it adds only 4-11 leaves a year.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Agave lechuguilla: 50% germination in ~4 days at 25-30 C; 3.9-10.8 new leaves/plant/yr; rosette of 20-50 leaves, 20-60 cm; leaves live 12-15 yr; flowers once, typically at 10-20 yr (stalk 1-4 m), then dies and is replaced by clones; rhizomes ~10 cm deep; seedlings rarely observed. Rosette size-age estimated.

ground.name: Welwitschia
ground.source: Welwitschia mirabilis, Namib Desert fog belt, two strap leaves on a woody stump, 0.3-1 m — SANBI PlantZAfrica

traits.native_range: Welwitschia mirabilis, Namib Desert fog belt, two strap leaves on a woody stump, 0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: two long shredded straps on a stump

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two strap-like cotyledons 25-35 mm long, pink at first then green, lie on the sand; between them the only two true leaves appear, broad grey-green straps that keep growing from their base for the plant's whole life. For years it is a flat cross of four blades over a deep taproot; the woody, two-lobed, dish-like crown widens slowly and the leaves fray into ribbons.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Welwitschia): only two leaves, growing continuously to 4 m, crown up to about 1 m across, many plants hundreds of years old, the oldest perhaps 2000; cotyledons 25-35 mm, pink turning green; dioecious, green to salmon or brown cones, pollinated mainly by flies. Germination, spread curve (height_years), crown emergence and first coning estimated.

ground.name: Hard spinifex
ground.source: Triodia basedowii, dominant hummock grass of the central Australian sand deserts, 30-100 cm rings — Flora of Australia

traits.native_range: Triodia basedowii, dominant hummock grass of the central Australian sand deserts, 30-100 cm rings — Flora of Australia
traits.leaf_shape: narrow grass blades in a dense tussock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling (it regrows only from seed after fire): a small tuft of thin grass blades, soft and green at first, soon rolled into stiff, sharp, grey-green needles. Tillers spread outward into a low dense dome of spiny needles; after 20-40 unburnt years the centre dies and the hummock opens into a ring, then broken arcs, several metres across.
growth.source: WA DPIRD 'Insights into spinifex (Triodia) pastures' (T. basedowii rings 40-50 yr old; hard spinifex seeds 4-5 yr after fire); Lewandrowski et al. 2018 Ann. Bot. (Triodia germination, t50 about 3 d, dormancy broken by karrikin); Macquarie Univ. spinifex page (rings common 25+ yr after fire).

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings appear within days of rain as tiny grey-green tufts of narrow leaves. The plant quickly builds a stiff, much-branched tussock of cane-like, glaucous, jointed stems with short, sparse leaves, woody at the base, often catching wind-blown sand into a low mound around itself.
growth.source: Estimated from its ecology as a long-lived, rain-triggered Saharo-Arabian desert bunchgrass (tussocks to 1 m, woody culms, sand-trapping hummocks) and from Panicum germination data (FEIS P. virgatum)
